target_customer: Small satellite operators that need to reach orbits rideshare launches do not serve, up to geostationary orbit
problem: Rideshare launches drop small satellites in fixed low orbits, so operators cannot reach their target orbit cheaply and satellites without engines cannot move.
business_model: Per mission service selling orbit transfer vehicle rides and end to end satellite support

founders.name: Ignacio Belieres Montero
founders.background_notes: Listed as sole founder on the YC page. A DPL News article dated 2025-02-20 calls him a 27 year old Argentine engineer. A search snippet says he studied aerospace engineering at Stanford, not confirmed in an opened source so education left empty.

competitors.name: Momentus
competitors.what: Vigoride orbital transfer vehicle for last mile delivery of rideshare payloads up to 250 kg
competitors.traction_then: Contract with Exolaunch for smallsat LEO support announced February 2019

technical_complexity.rationale: Building a chemical propulsion spacecraft with its own bus, communications and flight software for a rideshare launch, as a small Argentine team with no local launch heritage, was research and hardware grade.

defensibility.rationale: Flight heritage and propulsion know how are hard to copy, but several tug startups pursued the same market and the services are commodity once working.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent acquired Epic. Rival tug companies such as D-Orbit and Momentus flew vehicles earlier or at larger scale.

market_need_then: Rideshare launches on Falcon 9 were growing and small satellite operators needed last mile transport, as shown by Momentus signing launch integrator deals in early 2019.

branding.domain_note: Uses epic-aerospace.com with a hyphen (source: company site URL).

identity.mascot_or_character: Vehicles named Chimera, a mythological hybrid creature
identity.voice_and_tone: celebratory, e.g. the site says WE ARE IN ORBIT

branding.community_and_virality: Coverage in Core Memory (2026-01) and Argentine press, mostly about the hardware rather than the brand.

brand_strength.rationale: Little brand specific coverage; the Chimera name adds a memorable product line but the company name is generic.

outcome_analysis: Epic Aerospace flew its first vehicle Chimera LEO 1 in January 2023 on a SpaceX rideshare and a GEO vehicle in February 2025 on an Intuitive Machines mission, though trackers suggest the first vehicle may not have worked. Public funding is thin and only aggregator figures exist. The company remains active with a small team, so the outcome is unresolved and execution on the hardware has been slow versus tug rivals.
notes: Funding unverified: aggregators list about $150K to $250K over 2 to 3 rounds including a Thiel Fellowship grant and a 2020 grant; sources conflict so no round is recorded. Founding year 2017 from a search summary, other databases say 2014, 2018 or 2019. Team size varies 14 to 33. The Core Memory piece is paywalled beyond its subtitle. Competitor list has one entry since only Momentus had a source dated near the batch. Completeness pass: the seed round rests on Seedtable and Bouncewatch (both $150K, August 2019); the grant rests on a single database (CB Insights, about $100K, 2020-12-30, which totals $250K over 3 rounds, so one round is unidentified). Persana lists a Seed in February 2021 with no amount. No press source found.
